title: The ‘madness’ of Valeriya Novodvorskaya
gist: A portrait of Russian dissident Valeriya Novodvorskaya, jailed as 'insane' by the Soviet state and later used by Putin's Kremlin-controlled media as a caricature of liberalism, showing how pathologising opponents serves authoritarian regimes in both eras.

insights.claim: Soviet authorities institutionalised psychiatric detention of dissidents from the late 1950s, using the invented diagnosis 'sluggish schizophrenia' (symptoms such as conflict with authorities or fixation on political ideas) to detain people indefinitely without trial and strip them of credibility.
insights.speaker: Erik W. Larsson
insights.so_what: Historical template for how authoritarian states discredit opponents; useful when assessing repression risk in Russia.
insights.locator: Incarcerating political dissidents in mental hospitals

insights.claim: Novodvorskaya was arrested at 18 or so after scattering anti-Party leaflets at a Kremlin opera, spent two years in the Kazan psychiatric prison hospital, was treated with high-dose haloperidol, and was repeatedly rehospitalised through the 1970s for samizdat activity.
insights.speaker: Erik W. Larsson
insights.so_what: Illustrates the long reach of Soviet coercive psychiatry.
insights.locator: A year later, hundreds of guests gathered in the Kremlin

insights.claim: After 1991 the term 'demshiza' (democrat plus schizophrenia) was used pejoratively for fanatical reformers, and Novodvorskaya's radicalism, Ayn Rand-style libertarianism and Hitler comparisons made her its personification, undermining liberal credibility.
insights.speaker: Erik W. Larsson
insights.so_what: Liberal opposition in Russia was weakened by internal marginalisation, not only repression.
insights.locator: Public scepticism about activists like Novodvorskaya

insights.claim: Novodvorskaya warned in 2000 that Putin and his KGB associates would end democracy, but was dismissed as alarmist even by democracy activists who saw Putin as an ardent democrat restoring order.
insights.speaker: Erik W. Larsson
insights.so_what: Early warnings about Putin were dismissed; a reminder that consensus on Russian regime intent lagged reality.
insights.locator: When Putin first came to power in 2000

insights.claim: By late 2003 all major Russian television stations were state-controlled, and the Kremlin benefited from presenting Novodvorskaya as the face of liberalism so that opposition parties and leaders looked unbalanced, as in the 2003 shouting match with Zhirinovsky on a Solovyov talk show.
insights.speaker: Erik W. Larsson
insights.so_what: State media shapes opposition perception; the manufactured choice of 'Putin or chaos' underpins regime stability.
insights.locator: In the years that followed, Putin's government tightened its grip

insights.claim: Novodvorskaya claimed that at best five per cent of Russians espoused democracy and individual freedom in the European tradition, a bleak view of domestic demand for liberalism.
insights.speaker: Erik W. Larsson
insights.so_what: An opinionated dissident estimate, not a measured statistic; indicates pessimism about Russian liberal constituencies.
insights.locator: Not everything said about Novodvorskaya is true

insights.claim: The author concludes that under the Soviets she was locked away for being mad and under Putin was put on television for the same reason, showing how both regimes used the label of madness against her.
insights.speaker: Erik W. Larsson
insights.so_what: Continuity of delegitimisation tactics across Russian regimes.
insights.quote: In the Soviet Union, she was locked away for being mad; under Putin, she was put on television for the very same reason.
